feedback: Written before this candidate has raced, so no result is stated for it. What I had to do in the controller: a larger wheel raises turn rate per unit PWM difference by about 17 percent (0.035/0.030), so I lowered kp from 0.8 to 0.7 and kept kd 0.15, ki 0, base_speed 1.5 and last_direction. Evidence: iteration 7 (1.0 kg, 0.030 m wheels) scored 73.33, the best so far, with max_error 0.060 to 0.066 m and RMS 0.019 to 0.036 m, so the peak is a bend transient. Iteration 4 showed that a change in effective turn gain without matching kp lowers bend progress (s-bend 0.156 to 0.081), so the kp match matters. Decision rules for the next race: if the score is above 73.33 and oval and slalom progress rise, keep 0.035 m and try wheel_radius 0.040 m next. If the score falls while max_error is unchanged and progress stays flat, the ground-speed gain is not the lever, so return to 0.030 m and test sensor_size 0.016 m. If steering_oscillation rises above about 0.18 on the s-bend or slalom, the effective gain is still too high, so change kp in the controller, not the geometry.
requested_changes: If wheel_radius 0.035 m beats 73.33 with progress rising on the oval and slalom, try wheel_radius 0.040 m with everything else unchanged. Iterations 3 to 7 reached only 0.12 to 0.23 of the course, so more ground speed at the same PWM is the main lever left (a hypothesis from the progress shortfall, not yet measured).

If wheel_radius 0.035 m falls below 73.33 while max_error is unchanged at 0.060 to 0.066 m, return to wheel_radius 0.030 m and try sensor_size 0.016 m on the 80 mm row. The slalom has shown 2.0 line-loss events in iterations 0, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and a larger footprint keeps readings above the 0.05 line-loss threshold for longer (iteration 1 changed sensor size with other variables, so this is unproven).

If the larger wheel raises s-bend or slalom steering_oscillation above about 0.18 (iteration 7 values 0.177 and 0.168), keep wheel_radius 0.035 m and try mass 1.2 kg alone. Mass rose monotonically from 0.6 to 1.0 kg (55.4, 69.2, 73.3), so a heavier robot may add the yaw damping that the higher effective gain needs.
